# Motivation  

The Colorado division of Fire Prevention and Control reports that, in recorded Colorado history, "20 of 20 largest wildfires have occurred in the last 20 years". Furthermore they show that the three largest fires in Colorado occurred in 2020 and burned more than 500,000 acres. Are these extreme fire events more likely to occur in Colorado under current climate than the climate of 50 years ago? To provide a useful answer that question we perform an extreme event attribution study for fire weather in Colorado. In particular we consider the climate just north of Grand Lake, CO which was burned in the East Troublesome fire in 2020 (the second largest fire in Colorado history).

# Data 

## ERA5

We consider ERA5 reanalysis data downloaded from the Copernicus Climate Change Service on the grid cell including latitude 40.25 degrees and longitude -105.75 degrees.  This area was chosen due to its proximity to one of the largest fires in 2020 and the location of a weather station so that we could replicate our results with a second data set. We downloaded hourly ten meter wind speed in the U and V directions, two meter dew point, two meter temperature, and total precipitation for the months of June through October for all available years (1959 - 2021). These months were chosen as they encompass Colorado's fire season and they match the season chosen in a previous study (Mhatre and Cooley, in progress). These five variables were used to compute the daily Fire Weather Index (FWI).  
  
The Canadian fire weather index (FWI) is a function of the time series' of daily screen level temperature, screen level relative humidity, ten-meter wind speed, and 24-hour accumulated precipitation. To compute the FWI one must first use the four weather variables to compute three fuel moisture codes and two fire behavior indices. These five sub-indices are combined to compute a single value which indicates how likely a fire is to start and how quickly it could spread each day. We note that a benefit of using FWI is that the only signal that it contains is a climate signal and thus any difference that we notice must be due to some change in the marginal climate distribution rather than forest management or other potential confounders.

## RAWS  

We consider RAWS data (... to come ...)  
  
# Big Picture  
  
To determine whether a fire season like 2020's is more or less likely under current and past climate we use transformed linear models for time series extremes. These time series models were chosen because we are interested in the dependence in the upper tail of the distribution. We are not interested in modeling the bulk of the distribution (classical time series) as the bulk does not adequately inform about these extreme events. Many other extreme value time series models either model dependence in both tails (unhelpful in this case) or model the upper tail with strict modeling assumptions. These models restrict attention to the upper tail through the use of transformed linear operations (Cooley and Thibaud) and are determined by the tail pairwise dependence function (TPDF) (Mahtre and Cooley, in progress).  
  
Before using these models we must transform the marginal distribution for our time series to be non-negative regularly varying with tail index 2 and the time series must exhibit weak tail stationarity. FWI is non-negative but exploratory analysis indicate that the our time series has a bounded tail. Exploratory analysis suggest seasonality in the upper quantiles of the FWI time series. This seasonality must be removed.  
  
To satisfy the requirements of the models we estimate the seasonality and transform the marginal distribution to be uniform with the probability integral transform. Once the time series is marginally uniform we transform the time series to be marginally Frechet with scale 1 and tail index $\alpha = 2$.   
  
We then estimate the TPDF and run Mhatre and Cooley's analogue to the innovations algorithm which provides as many moving average (MA) parameters as needed to adequately model the tail dependence. These parameter estimates are then used to simulate new seasons. Summary statistics and TPDF plots are used to determine the order of the MA(q).   
  
Once we have an adequate model for the tail dependence we simulate 10,000 seasons of FWI time series under both current and past climate. We then compute the probability of seeing as many days above the 0.95 quantile of current climate FWI as we saw in 2020.   
  
  
# Estimation of Seasonality  

```{r "marginal distribution estimation", cache = T, echo = F, warning=FALSE}
file.name <- "ERA5_data/ERA5_CO_FWI_07_15.csv"

# The following are the values that we must choose for forward and back transformation
past <- 1959:1978
present <- 2002:2021
gpd_quant <- 0.975 # quantile for gpd in original marginal estimation
window_size <- 14 # number of days on each side of the moving window for marginal estimation 
maxlag <- 30 # How many lags to estimate tpdf 
r0_quant <- 0.975 # high radial quantile for tpdf estimation 
set.seed(92432) # noise sequence seed
seq_length <- 50000 # length of noise sequence to generate MA(q)'s for fitting
max_theta <- maxlag # maximum reasonable order of for MA(q)
chosen_order <- 15 # what order MA(q) do we want to use 


#load the data 
data.temp <- read_csv(file.name, show_col_types = FALSE)

#restrict to months we are considering
data.temp <- filter(data.temp, MON %in% 6:10)

#restrict to years we are considering 
data_early <- filter(data.temp, YR %in% past)
data_late <- filter(data.temp, YR %in% present)


#Get rid of "bad" years (bad if it has fewer than 50 days or fewer than 5 observations above some value)
keep <- c()

#past climate
 #0.7 quantile of past FWI used to determine if a year has enough moderately high observations 
      # to considered a full year   
quant_good <- quantile(data_early$FWI, probs = 0.7) 
for(yr in unique(data_early$YR)){
  data_temp <- filter(data_early, YR == yr)
  if((length(data_temp$FWI) > 50) && (sum(data_temp$FWI > quant_good) >= 5)){
    keep <- c(keep, yr)
  } 
}

data_early <- filter(data_early, YR %in% keep)

#current climate
keep <- c()

for(yr in unique(data_late$YR)){
  data_temp <- filter(data_late, YR == yr)
  if((length(data_temp$FWI) > 50) && (sum(data_temp$FWI > quant_good) >= 5)){
    keep <- c(keep, yr)
  } 
}

data_late <- filter(data_late, YR %in% keep)

# Add a variable "days_since" to represent days since June 1
data_early$days_since <- as.numeric(data_early$DATE - as.Date(paste(data_early$YR, "-05-31", sep = "")))
data_late$days_since <- as.numeric(data_late$DATE - as.Date(paste(data_late$YR, "-05-31", sep = "")))
data_late_no2020 <- data_late[-c(which(data_late$YR == 2020)),]

# save quantiles (i.e. sort the (2k+1) day moving window of observations for each day)
ecdf_early <- matrix(NA, nrow = (2*window_size+1)*20, ncol = 153)
ecdf_late <- matrix(NA, nrow = (2*window_size+1)*20, ncol = 153)
ecdf_late_no2020 <- matrix(NA, nrow = (2*window_size+1)*20, ncol = 153)

for(i in 1:153){
  # consider only days between day i-k and i+k and sort the values on those (2k+1) days
  temp_data_early <- sort(data_early$FWI[which(data_early$days_since %in% 
                                      max(1, i-window_size):min(153, i+window_size))])
  temp_data_late <- sort(data_late$FWI[which(data_late$days_since %in% 
                                      max(1, i-window_size):min(153, i+window_size))])
  temp_data_late_no2020 <- sort(data_late_no2020$FWI[which(data_late_no2020$days_since %in% 
                                      max(1, i-window_size):min(153, i+window_size))])
  
  # save the sorted days within the moving window as the ecdf quantiles
  ecdf_early[1:length(temp_data_early), i] <- temp_data_early
  ecdf_late[1:length(temp_data_late), i] <- temp_data_late
  ecdf_late_no2020[1:length(temp_data_late_no2020), i] <- temp_data_late_no2020
}


# save the threshold values
mu_early <- mu_late <- mu_late_no2020 <- rep(NA, 153)

for (i in 1:153){
  q_temp_early <- floor(gpd_quant*(1+length(na.omit(ecdf_early[,i]))))
  mu_early[i] <- ecdf_early[q_temp_early, i]
  
  q_temp_late <- floor(gpd_quant*(1+length(na.omit(ecdf_late[,i]))))
  mu_late[i] <- ecdf_late[q_temp_late, i]
  
  q_temp_late_no_2020 <- floor(gpd_quant*(1+length(na.omit(ecdf_late_no2020[,i]))))
  mu_late_no2020[i] <- ecdf_late_no2020[q_temp_late_no_2020, i]
}

# Compute and save the amount that observations exceed the threshold. 
exceedance_early <- exceedance_late <- exceedance_late_no2020 <- c()
yrs_early <- yrs_late <- yrs_late_no2020 <- c()
days_early <- days_late <- days_late_no2020 <- c()

for (i in 1:153){
  indices_temp <- which(data_early$days_since == i) #take all of the ith days
  temp_data_early <- data_early$FWI[indices_temp] 
  temp_ex_early <- temp_data_early - mu_early[i] #compute exceedances
  exceedance_early <- c(exceedance_early, temp_ex_early) #append
  yrs_early <- c(yrs_early, data_early$YR[indices_temp])
  days_early <- c(days_early, rep(i, length(indices_temp)))
  
  indices_temp <- which(data_late$days_since == i)
  temp_data_late <- data_late$FWI[indices_temp]
  temp_ex_late <- temp_data_late - mu_late[i]
  exceedance_late <- c(exceedance_late, temp_ex_late)
  yrs_late <- c(yrs_late, data_late$YR[indices_temp])
  days_late <- c(days_late, rep(i, length(indices_temp)))
  
  indices_temp <- which(data_late_no2020$days_since == i)
  temp_data_late_no2020 <- data_late_no2020$FWI[indices_temp]
  temp_ex_late_no2020 <- temp_data_late_no2020 - mu_late_no2020[i]
  exceedance_late_no2020 <- c(exceedance_late_no2020, temp_ex_late_no2020)
  yrs_late_no2020 <- c(yrs_late_no2020, data_late_no2020$YR[indices_temp])
  days_late_no2020 <- c(days_late_no2020, rep(i, length(indices_temp)))
}

# Rearrange exceedances so that they are in the same order as the data
exceedance_early <- data.frame(exceedance_early, yrs_early, days_early) %>% arrange(yrs_early)
exceedance_late <- data.frame(exceedance_late, yrs_late, days_late) %>% arrange(yrs_late)
exceedance_late_no2020 <- data.frame(exceedance_late_no2020, yrs_late_no2020, days_late_no2020) %>% arrange(yrs_late_no2020)

# fit the GPD to the exceedances and save the likelihood value
single_model_early <- fpot(exceedance_early$exceedance_early, threshold = 0)
single_model_late <- fpot(exceedance_late$exceedance_late, threshold = 0)
single_model_late_no2020 <- fpot(exceedance_late_no2020$exceedance_late_no2020, threshold = 0)

#save parameter values
scale_early <- unname(single_model_early$estimate[1])
shape_early <- unname(single_model_early$estimate[2])
scale_late <- unname(single_model_late$estimate[1])
shape_late <- unname(single_model_late$estimate[2])

scale_late_no2020 <- unname(single_model_late_no2020$estimate[1])
shape_late_no2020 <- unname(single_model_late_no2020$estimate[2])

### Transform to uniform
#column is year
ts_uniform_early <- ts_uniform_late <- ts_uniform_late_no2020 <- matrix(NA, nrow = 153, ncol = 20) 

#early
for(i in 1:length(data_early$FWI)){
  j <- data_early$days_since[i]
  yr <- which(unique(data_early$YR) == data_early$YR[i])
  if(data_early$FWI[i] < mu_early[j]) {
    ts_uniform_early[j, yr] <- which(ecdf_early[,j] == data_early$FWI[i]) /
      (length(na.omit(ecdf_early[,j]))+1)
  } else {
    ts_uniform_early[j, yr] <- gpd_quant + (1-gpd_quant) * pgpd(data_early$FWI[i], 
                                                    loc = mu_early[j],
                                                    scale = single_model_early$estimate[1], 
                                                    shape = single_model_early$estimate[2])
  }
}

#late
for(i in 1:length(data_late$FWI)){
  j <- data_late$days_since[i]
  yr <- which(unique(data_late$YR) == data_late$YR[i])
  if(data_late$FWI[i] < mu_late[j]) {
    ts_uniform_late[j, yr] <- which(ecdf_late[,j] == data_late$FWI[i]) /
      (length(na.omit(ecdf_late[,j]))+1)
  } else {
    ts_uniform_late[j, yr] <- gpd_quant + (1-gpd_quant) * pgpd(data_late$FWI[i], 
                                                   loc = mu_late[j],
                                                   scale = single_model_late$estimate[1], 
                                                   shape = single_model_late$estimate[2])
  }
}

#late_no2020
for(i in 1:length(data_late_no2020$FWI)){
  j <- data_late_no2020$days_since[i]
  yr <- which(unique(data_late_no2020$YR) == data_late_no2020$YR[i])
  if(data_late_no2020$FWI[i] < mu_late_no2020[j]) {
    ts_uniform_late_no2020[j, yr] <- which(ecdf_late_no2020[,j] == data_late_no2020$FWI[i]) /
      (length(na.omit(ecdf_late_no2020[,j]))+1)
  } else {
    ts_uniform_late_no2020[j, yr] <- gpd_quant + (1-gpd_quant) * pgpd(data_late_no2020$FWI[i], 
                                                   loc = mu_late_no2020[j],
                                                   scale = single_model_late_no2020$estimate[1], 
                                                   shape = single_model_late_no2020$estimate[2])
  }
}


############
#Frechet with alpha=2
###########
RV_ts_early <- 1/sqrt(log(1/ts_uniform_early))
RV_ts_late <- 1/sqrt(log(1/ts_uniform_late))
RV_ts_late_no2020 <- 1/sqrt(log(1/ts_uniform_late_no2020))


# Subtract mean (Bias correction)
me <- mean(na.omit(c(RV_ts_early)))
ml <- mean(na.omit(c(RV_ts_late)))
ml_no2020 <- mean(na.omit(c(RV_ts_late_no2020)))

RV_ts_early <- ifelse(RV_ts_early - me > 0,
                      RV_ts_early - me, 0)
RV_ts_late <- ifelse(RV_ts_late - ml > 0,
                     RV_ts_late - ml, 0)
RV_ts_late_no2020 <- ifelse(RV_ts_late_no2020 - ml_no2020 > 0,
                     RV_ts_late_no2020 - ml_no2020, 0)

``` 

  
The first step in much of time series analysis is a determination on whether a given time series is stationary. To explore tail stationarity we first look for evidence of seasonality by comparing high quantiles of the marginal distribution for each day. Our data has 63 observations of each calendar day which implies that if we restrict attention to each individual day our high quantile estimates will be very noise (figure 1). It is reasonable to borrow strength from surrounding days to decrease the variance in quantile estimation. This borrowing of strength will increase the bias in the estimation of the marginal. We readily accept the increased bias because we think that the bias introduced will be minimal; it is unlikely that the marginal distribution of weather on July 15 is meaningfully different from that of July 16 or July 22. 

```{r "seasonality plot 1", echo = F, fig.cap = "97.5th quantile of FWI by day (1959-2021). Noisy estimate (black) from only using that day's observations. Smoothed estimate (blue) from including observations from seven days before and after the date being estimated (ex. to estimate July 15th we include all observations between July 8th and July 22nd).", fig.height= 3}
# first we make a plot of the daily 0.95 quantile when considering all years
quantiles_95_per_day <- rep(NA, 153)
seasonality_quantile <- 0.975
num_days <- c(30, 31, 31, 30, 31)
num_days_in_prev_months <- 0
for (i in 6:10){
  num_days_this_month <- num_days[(i-5)]
  for (j in 1:num_days_this_month){
    quantiles_95_per_day[j + num_days_in_prev_months] <- quantile(filter(data.temp, MON == i,
                                                                         DAY == j)$FWI,
                                                                  seasonality_quantile, type = 1)
  }
  num_days_in_prev_months <- num_days_in_prev_months + num_days_this_month
}

k <- 15
q <- c(0.25, 0.5, 0.7, 0.85, 0.975)

data.temp$days_since <- rep(seq(0,152,1), length(unique(data.temp$YR)))
quant <- matrix(NA, nrow = (154-k), ncol=5)
means <- rep(NA, 154-k)

for (i in 0:(153-k-1)) {
  temp <- filter(data.temp, days_since %in% c(i:(i+k)))$FWI
  quant[(i+1),] <- quantile(temp, q, type = 1, na.rm = T)
  means[(i+1)] <- mean(temp)
}

plot(quantiles_95_per_day, type = "l",
     xlab = "Days Since June 1", ylab = "FWI")
lines(8:146, quant[,5], col = "blue")
```
  
Cursory quantile plots suggest the presence of bi-modal seasonality in the high quantiles of daily FWI (figure 1). We note that this bi-modal seasonality remains when we split the data used for estimation into what we consider past climate (1959 - 1978) and present climate (2002 - 2021) (figures 2 and 3). We note that there appears to be a shift in the high quantiles between the two time periods and thus expect a season like 2020 to be more likely under current climate.

# Estimation of the Marginal distribution 

We estimate the marginal distribution of daily fire weather through a day-dependent moving window empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF) for the bulk of the distribution and a day-dependent generalized pareto distribution for the upper tail. We estimate the marginal distribution separately for present and past climate. To estimate the marginal distribution of present climate on day $t$ we use all observations from $t-k$ through $t+k$ in years 2002 through 2021 to compute the day dependent ECDF. Wu use the day-dependent ECDF to compute the 0.975 quantile $\hat{\mu}_t^{present}$ which is our threshold for the GPD. Points above the threshold are modeled with a GPD with scale and shape estimates $\hat{\psi}^{present}$ and $\hat{\xi}^{present}$ respectively:  

$$ \hat{F}_t^{present} (x) = \begin{cases} 
      \{20(2k+1) + 1\}^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^{20} \sum_{j = t-k}^{t+k} \mathbb{I}(x_{ij} > x) & x\leq \hat{\mu}_{t}^{present} \\
      1 - 0.025\left\{1+\hat{\xi}^{present}(x-\hat{\mu}_{t}^{present}) / \hat{\psi}^{present}\right\}^{-1/ \hat{\xi}^{present}} & x > \hat{\mu}_{t} 
   \end{cases}$$

The marginal for past climate was estimated in the same way. We considered allowing the scale and shape parameters of the GPD to vary by time as well but likelihood ratio tests and plots of the estimated parameters suggested that this was unwarranted.  

```{r "gpd parameter table", echo = F, fig.cap= "GPD parameter estimates"}
parameter <- c("scale", "shape")
past_paras <- c(scale_early, shape_early)
present_paras <- c(scale_late, shape_late)

gpd_paras <- data.frame("." = parameter, "past" = round(past_paras, 4), "present" = round(present_paras, 4))

kable(gpd_paras)
```
  
# Dependence Estimation  
  
Once the marginal distribution of the two climate periods has been estimated we transform the data to be marginally Frechet distributed with scale one and shape parameter $\alpha = 2$. This means that the data is now non-negative regularly varying with tail index $2$. Furthermore we can reasonably assume that the time series are weakly tail stationary and thus we can estimate the tail dependence with an ajusted version of the TPDF estimator of Cooley and Thibaud. Unlike previous studies (Mhatre and Cooley, in progress) we do not have a single time series but 20 observed time series of each climate period. This separation into 20 time series is necessary because we do not expect the tail dependence between July 15th, 2002 and July 16th, 2002 to be the same as the tail dependence between October 31st, 2002 and June 1st, 2003 for obvious reasons.   
  
Due to this complication we adjust Cooley and Thibaud's estimator by computing the radial components separately by year and then combine the radial components into one vector to compute the TPDF. Let $(x_{y,t}, x_{y,t+h})$ be the year $y$ lag-$h$ pairs of observations from a weakly tail stationary time series $\{X_{y.t}\}$. Consider $r_{y,t} = \lVert (x_{y,t}, x_{y,t+h})\lVert _2$, the $l-2$ distance from the origin to the point $(x_{y,t}, x_{y,t+h})$ (the radial components). Finally consider $(w_{y,t}, w_{y,t+h}) = (x_{y,t}, x_{y,t+h})/r_{y,t}$, the unit-radius points. Our TPDF estimator is defined as 

$$ \hat{\sigma}(h) = \frac{2}{\sum_{y=1}^{20}\sum_{t = 1}^{n-h}\mathbb{I}(r_{y,t} > r_0)} \sum_{y=1}^{20}\sum_{t = 1}^{n-h}  w_{y,t} w_{y,t+h} \mathbb{I}(r_{y,t} > r_0) $$  
  
Where $r_0$ is some high quantile of all radial components $r_{y,t}$, $y = 1, 2, ..., 20$ and $t = 1, 2, ... , n-h$. 

 
```{r "tpdf estimation", echo = F, cache = T}
#########
#Estimate TPDF
#########

# compute lags
lags_early <- lags_late <- matrix(NA, nrow = (153*20), ncol = maxlag+1)

for(i in 1:20){
  indices <- c(((i-1)*153+1):(i*153))
  lags_early[indices, (maxlag+1)] <- RV_ts_early[,i] #save transformed data into a vector
  lags_late[indices, (maxlag+1)] <- RV_ts_late[,i]
  for(j in 1:maxlag){
    lags_early[indices, j] <- lag(RV_ts_early[,i], j) 
    #append each years lagged vectors onto previous years
    lags_late[indices, j] <- lag(RV_ts_late[,i], j)
  }
}

# compute radial components
rt_early <- rt_late <- matrix(NA, nrow <- (153*20), ncol = maxlag)

for(j in 1:maxlag){
  rt_early[,j] <- sqrt(lags_early[,j]^2 + lags_early[,(maxlag+1)]^2)
  
  rt_late[,j] <- sqrt(lags_late[,j]^2 + lags_late[,(maxlag+1)]^2)
}

# compute "high threshold of radial component" (0.95 quantile of radial components)
r0_early <- r0_late <- rep(NA, maxlag)

for (i in 1:maxlag){
  len <- length(na.omit(rt_early[,i]))
  ind <- floor(r0_quant*len)
  r0_early[i] <- sort(na.omit(rt_early[,i]))[ind]
  
  len <- length(na.omit(rt_late[,i]))
  ind <- floor(r0_quant*len)
  r0_late[i] <- sort(na.omit(rt_late[,i]))[ind]
}


# Compute tpdf
tpdf_early <- tpdf_late <- rep(NA, maxlag)

for (i in 1:maxlag) {
  wi_temp <- lags_early[,i]*lags_early[,(maxlag+1)]/(rt_early[,i]^2) #angular components
  rt_temp <- ifelse(is.na(rt_early[,i]), 0, rt_early[,i]) #set NA's to zer
  k <- sum(rt_temp > r0_early[i]) # how many above radial threshold
  tpdf_early[i] <- 2/k * sum(wi_temp[which(rt_temp>r0_early[i])])
  
  wi_temp <- lags_late[,i]*lags_late[,(maxlag+1)]/(rt_late[,i]^2) #angular components
  rt_temp <- ifelse(is.na(rt_late[,i]), 0, rt_late[,i]) #set NA's to zer
  k <- sum(rt_temp > r0_late[i]) # how many above radial threshold
  tpdf_late[i] <- 2/k * sum(wi_temp[which(rt_temp>r0_late[i])])
}

#add lag 0 to tpdf
tpdf_early <- c(1, tpdf_early)
tpdf_late <- c(1, tpdf_late)  
```

# Model Estimation   

Mhatre and Cooley (in progress) developed transformed linear extreme value analogues to classical $MA(q)$, $AR(p)$, and $ARMA(p,q)$ time series models. In their development of the $ARMA(p,q)$ models they show that the unique stationary solution is an $MA(\infty)$ and thus the TPDF is well approximated by the TPDF of a large order $MA(q)$. Mhartre and Cooley (in progress) developed an analogue to the innovations algorithm which, like the classical innovations algorithm, can be used to estimate parameters of an $MA(\infty)$ with the same TPDF as the weakly tail stationary, regularly varying time series with tail index $\alpha = 2$. This extremes innovation algorithm is deterministic, computationally cheap, and very flexible which is why we use it to estimate a set of thetas which have the same TPDF as the empirical TPDF.  
  
```{r "innovations parameter estimation", echo = F}
####
# Estimate theta's using innovations algorithm
####
nu_early <- nu_late <- rep(NA, maxlag+1)
theta_hat_early <- theta_hat_late <- matrix(0, nrow = maxlag, ncol = maxlag)

   # note that nu[5] is the fourth iteration because r does not have index 0
nu_early[1] <- tpdf_early[1] 
nu_late[1] <- tpdf_late[1]

for(n in 1:maxlag){
  for(k in 0:(n-1)){
    temp_sum_early <- 0
    temp_sum_late <- 0 
    if(k>0){
      for(j in 0:(k-1)){
        temp_sum_early <- temp_sum_early + theta_hat_early[k, k-j]*
          theta_hat_early[n, n-j]*nu_early[j+1]
        
        temp_sum_late <- temp_sum_late + theta_hat_late[k, k-j]*
          theta_hat_late[n, n-j]*nu_late[j+1]
      }
    }
    theta_hat_early[n, n-k] <- nu_early[k+1]^(-1) * 
      (tpdf_early[n-k+1] - temp_sum_early)
    
    theta_hat_late[n, n-k] <- nu_late[k+1]^(-1) * 
      (tpdf_late[n-k+1] - temp_sum_late)
  }
  
  nu_early[n+1] <- nu_early[1]
  nu_late[n+1] <- nu_late[1]
  for(l in 0:(n-1)){
    nu_early[n+1] <- nu_early[n+1] - theta_hat_early[n, (n-l)]^2*nu_early[l+1] 
    
    nu_late[n+1] <- nu_late[n+1] - theta_hat_late[n, (n-l)]^2*nu_late[l+1] 
  }
}
```

# Choosing Order of $MA(q)$  

We choose which order, $q$, to use by looking at the TPDF and by comparing summary statistics from our data to the same summary statistics given by fitted models of reasonable orders. In particular, we consider the mean run length above high quantiles ($0.95, 0.975, and 0.99$) as well as high quantiles of the sum of 5 consecutive terms. If we have estimated the marginal correctly and have modeled the tail dependence usefully then we should be able to match these two upper tail-dependent statistics.  
  


```{r "summary stats functions", cache = T, echo = F}
mean_run <- function(data, quant){
  # get quantile
  quant_temp <- quantile(probs = quant, data)
  
  # get indices above quantile
  runs_index <- which(data > unname(quant_temp))
  
  # convert vector of indices to matrix of runs
  runs_seq <- R.utils::seqToIntervals(runs_index)
  
  # Compute run lengths
  runs_length <- runs_seq[,2] - runs_seq[,1] + 1
  
  # return mean of the run lengths
  return(mean(runs_length))
}


sum_high_quant <- function(data, quant, m = 5){
  sum_of_m<- rep(NA, length(data)-m)

  # Compute sum of m consecutive terms
  for(i in 1:(length(data)-m)){
    sum_of_m[i] <- sum(data[i:(i+m-1)])
  }
  
  # return quantile of the sums
  return(quantile(sum_of_m, probs = quant))
}
```


```{r "summary stats on data", cache=T, echo = F}

mean_run_late[3] <- mean_run(data = data_late$FWI, quant = summary_quants[3])

sum_early[3] <- sum_high_quant(data = data_early$FWI, quant = summary_quants[3])

sum_late[2] <- sum_high_quant(data = data_late$FWI, quant = summary_quants[2])
sum_late[3] <- sum_high_quant(data = data_late$FWI, quant = summary_quants[3])

summary_stats <- data.frame(quantile = summary_quants, "mean past" = mean_run_early,

It is known that the empirical TPDF is a biased estimate of the true TPDF (figure 7). This introduces a non-trivial challenge when comparing our empirical TPDF to the TPDF calculated from the parameters estimated by the innovations algorithm. The innovations algorithm can fit any valid TPDF to any order with arbitrarily small error which means that we end up modelling the biased tail dependence thus we expect some difference in the aforementioned summary statistics. 
  
With this understanding we notice that the empirical TPDF plots seem to level out between lag 10 and lag 20 so we expect that a reasonable model order is somewhere in that range. To be conservative we compute summary statistics for simulated time series from $MA(q)$ models of orders $q = 1, 2, ..., 50$ and compare them to the values computed from our data (figures 8 & 9). We note that the different quantiles suggest different order models and that the $0.99$ quantile suggests use of lower order models. For this reason we consider an $MA(10)$ for both present and past climate. 
  
  
```{r "generate MA(q)s", cache=TRUE, echo=FALSE}
a = 1
set.seed(83745)
## generate ts for each "reasonable" order of MA(q) and convert to original marginal
for(j in 1:max_theta){

  # Past climate MA fitting 
  theta_temp_early <- theta_hat_early[j,1:j]
  temp_ts_early <- rep(0, seq_length)
  temp_ts_early[1] <- z[1]
  
  for(i in 2:seq_length){
    temp_early <- z[i]
    k <- min((i-1), length(theta_temp_early))
    for(l in 1:k){
      temp_early <- tadd(temp_early, tmult(theta_temp_early[l], z[i-l]))
    }
    temp_ts_early[i] <- temp_early
  }
  # uniform marginal
  temp_ts_early <- ecdf(temp_ts_early)(temp_ts_early) - 
    0.5*min(ecdf(temp_ts_early)(temp_ts_early))
  
  #FWI marginal
  for(i in 1:seq_length){
    if(temp_ts_early[i] < gpd_quant){
      temp_ts_early[i] <- quantile(na.omit(ecdf_early[,day_index[i]]), temp_ts_early[i])
    } else {
      temp_ts_early[i] <- qgpd(temp_ts_early[i], mu_early[day_index[i]],
                      scale = scale_early, shape = shape_early)
    }
  }
  
  MA_early_mat[,j] <- temp_ts_early

# Current climate MA fitting 
  theta_temp_late <- theta_hat_late[j,1:j]
  temp_ts_late <- rep(0, seq_length)
  temp_ts_late[1] <- z[1]
  
  for(i in 2:seq_length){
    temp_late <- z[i]
    k <- min((i-1), length(theta_temp_late))
    for(l in 1:k){
      temp_late <- tadd(temp_late, tmult(theta_temp_late[l], z[i-l]))
    }
    temp_ts_late[i] <- temp_late
  }
  
  # uniform marginal
  temp_ts_late <- ecdf(temp_ts_late)(temp_ts_late) - 
    0.5*min(ecdf(temp_ts_late)(temp_ts_late))
  
  #FWI marginal
  for(i in 1:seq_length){
    if(temp_ts_late[i] < gpd_quant){
      temp_ts_late[i] <- quantile(na.omit(ecdf_late[,day_index[i]]), temp_ts_late[i])
    } else {
      temp_ts_late[i] <- qgpd(temp_ts_late[i], mu_late[day_index[i]],
                        scale = scale_late, shape = shape_late)
    }
  }
  
  MA_late_mat[,j] <- temp_ts_late
}



```

plot(mean_run_late_sim[,2], ylab = "run length 0.975", xlab = "MA order")

# Attribution  
  
To answer the the attribution question we compare the empirical probability of observing a season with as many days above a threshold as we observed in 2020. We consider the thresholds that are the 0.95, 0.975, and 0.99 quantile of the present climate data. We compute the probabilities from 10,000 seasons that are simulated from the two climate models. 
  
According to our model the probability of observing a season with at least as many days above the 0.95, 0.975, and 0.99 quantiles of observed present climate FWI as were observed in 2020 is at least 24, 20, and 9 times higher under present climate as it was under past climate.   

```{r "generate season function", echo = F}
generate_season <- function(thetas, z){
  n <- length(thetas)
  ma <- rep(NA, 153)
  
  for(i in 1:153){
    ma[i] <- z[i+n]
    for(j in 1:n){
      ma[i] <- tadd(ma[i], tmult(thetas[j], z[i+n-j]))
    }
  }
  
  return(ma)
}
```

```{r "sim 10,000 seasons and trans to FWI scale", echo = F, cache = T}
set.seed(6346)
a <- 1
seasons_early <- seasons_late <- rep(NA, 153*10000)

for(i in 1:10000){
  index_start <- (i-1)*153 + 1
  z <- rfrechet(153 + chosen_order, loc = 0, scale = 1, shape = 2)
  seasons_early[index_start:(index_start + 152)] <- generate_season(z = z, 
                          thetas = theta_hat_early[chosen_order, 1:chosen_order])
  seasons_late[index_start:(index_start + 152)] <- generate_season(z=z, 
                          thetas = theta_hat_late[chosen_order, 1:chosen_order])
}

# uniform marginal
seasons_early <- ecdf(seasons_early)(seasons_early) - 
  0.5*min(ecdf(seasons_early)(seasons_early))

seasons_late <- ecdf(seasons_late)(seasons_late) - 
  0.5*min(ecdf(seasons_late)(seasons_late))

# FWI marginal
day_index <- rep(1:153, 10000)
for(i in 1:length(seasons_early)){
  if(seasons_early[i] < gpd_quant){
    seasons_early[i] <- quantile(na.omit(ecdf_early[,day_index[i]]), seasons_early[i])
  } else {
    seasons_early[i] <- qgpd(seasons_early[i], mu_early[day_index[i]],
                      scale = scale_early, shape = shape_early)
  }
}

for(i in 1:length(seasons_late)){
  if(seasons_late[i] < gpd_quant){
    seasons_late[i] <- quantile(na.omit(ecdf_late[,day_index[i]]), seasons_late[i])
  } else {
    seasons_late[i] <- qgpd(seasons_late[i], mu_late[day_index[i]],
                      scale = scale_late, shape = shape_late)
  }
}

# split back into seasons
early_seasons <- late_seasons <- matrix(NA, nrow = 10000, ncol = 153)
for(i in 1:10000){
  index_start <- (i-1)*153 + 1
  early_seasons[i,] <- seasons_early[index_start:(index_start + 152)]
  late_seasons[i,] <- seasons_late[index_start:(index_start + 152)]
}
```
  
```{r, echo = F, cache = T}
present_tholds <- quantile(data_late$FWI, prob = summary_quants)
a <- 2
num_days_2020 <- rep(NA, 3)

for(i in 1:3){
  temp <- filter(data_late, YR == 2020)$FWI
  num_days_2020[i] <- length(which(temp > present_tholds[i]))
}

count_present_seasons <- rep(0, 3)
count_past_seasons <- rep(0,3)

for(j in 1:3){
  for(i in 1:10000){
    if (length(which(early_seasons[i,] > present_tholds[j])) >= num_days_2020[j]){
      count_past_seasons[j] <- count_past_seasons[j] + 1
    }
    if (length(which(late_seasons[i,] > present_tholds[j])) >= num_days_2020[j]){
      count_present_seasons[j] <- count_present_seasons[j] + 1
    }
  }
}

df_attribution <- data.frame("t'hold" = present_tholds,
                             "Days in 2020" = num_days_2020,
                             "Past" = count_past_seasons/10000, 
                             "Present" = count_present_seasons/10000, 
                             "Ratio" = count_present_seasons/count_past_seasons)

kable(df_attribution)

```  
  
    
```{r "histogram of num days above quantile per year"}
num_days_above_quantile_per_year_data_early <- 
  num_days_above_quantile_per_year_data_late <- 
  matrix(NA, ncol = 3, nrow = 20)

quantiles_early <- unname(quantile(data_early$FWI, probs = c(0.95, 0.975, 0.99)))
quantiles_late <- unname(quantile(data_late$FWI, probs = c(0.95, 0.975, 0.99)))

for(i in 1:20){
  early_year <- 1958 + i
  late_year <- 2002 + i
  
  for(j in 1:3){
    num_days_above_quantile_per_year_data_early[i,j] <- 
      sum(data_early$FWI[which(data_early$YR == early_year)] > quantiles_early[j])
    num_days_above_quantile_per_year_data_late[i,j] <- 
      sum(data_late$FWI[which(data_late$YR == late_year)] > quantiles_late[j])
  }
}

hist(num_days_above_quantile_per_year_data_early[,2])
hist(num_days_above_quantile_per_year_data_late[,2])


num_days_above_quantile_per_year_simulated_early <- 
  num_days_above_quantile_per_year_simulated_late <- 
  matrix(NA, ncol = 3, nrow = 10000)

for(i in 1:10000){
  for(j in 1:3){
    num_days_above_quantile_per_year_simulated_early[i,j] <- 
      sum(early_seasons[i,] > quantiles_early[j])
    num_days_above_quantile_per_year_simulated_late[i,j] <- 
      sum(late_seasons[i,] > quantiles_late[j])
  }
}

colors <- c(rgb(255, 0, 0, max = 255, alpha = 125, names = "red50"),
            rgb(0, 0, 255, max = 255, alpha = 125, names = "blue50"), 
            rgb(100, 0, 255, max = 255, alpha = 175, names = "bluered50"))

hist_quantile <- 1 # 1 is 0.95, 2 is 0.975, 3 is 0.99
hist_breaks   <- seq(0, 100, length.out = 101)


hist(num_days_above_quantile_per_year_data_early[,hist_quantile], xlim = c(0, 40),
     main = paste("Number of days above", summary_quants[hist_quantile],

legend("topright", legend = c("observed seasons", "simulated seasons", "overlap"), 
       bty = "n", text.col = colors, pch = 15, col = colors)
hist(num_days_above_quantile_per_year_data_late[,hist_quantile], xlim = c(0, 40),
